## June 23, 1956 — A Saturday at the Edge of Upheaval

You arrived on a Saturday in late June, into a summer that would prove to be one of the most turbulent in the Cold War era. The world was not at war, but it was not at peace either — and in the weeks and months ahead, it would come closer to breaking apart than most people at the time understood.

---

**Eighty-eight years before you were born, on this exact date, the typewriter was patented.** On June 23, 1868, Christopher Latham Sholes received his patent for the writing machine that would become the standard instrument of professional communication for nearly a century. By 1956, the typewriter was everywhere — in every office, every newsroom, every government building. It had shaped how language was produced and how information moved through institutions. In your lifetime, it went from ubiquitous to obsolete, replaced first by the word processor and then by the personal computer. You were born on the 88th anniversary of the device whose death you would witness.

**Five days after your birth, workers in Poznań rose up against communist rule — and were crushed.** On June 28, 1956, factory workers in the Polish city of Poznań took to the streets demanding better wages and conditions. The protest turned into an uprising. Polish army troops loyal to the Soviet-aligned government fired on the crowds; somewhere between 57 and 78 people were killed, hundreds wounded. The uprising was suppressed, but it sent a tremor through the communist bloc that would not stop. The same convulsion, amplified, would erupt in Hungary four months later. You were five days old when the first crack appeared.

**The Hungarian Revolution broke out four months after your birth.** On October 23, 1956, students and workers in Budapest took to the streets demanding Soviet withdrawal. For a few days, they appeared to be winning — the government promised reforms, Soviet troops withdrew from the capital. Then, on November 4, the tanks returned. The Red Army crushed the revolution in two weeks of street fighting. Two hundred thousand Hungarians fled the country as refugees. The West watched, issued statements, and did not intervene — the limits of Cold War rhetoric meeting Cold War reality, in real time, in the first months of your life.

**Thirty-three days after your birth, Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalized the Suez Canal.** On July 26, 1956, Egypt's president announced that the canal — built through Egyptian labor, running through Egyptian territory — now belonged to Egypt. Britain and France, who had controlled it for decades, began planning a military response. Israel, Britain, and France attacked in October. The United States and the Soviet Union both pressured them to stop — a moment that revealed that the old European empires now operated at the sufferance of the superpowers. Britain's Prime Minister resigned in January 1957. You were seven months old when the British Empire's effective end was confirmed.

**The hard disk drive was born in your birth year.** In September 1956, IBM shipped the first commercial magnetic hard disk drive — the RAMAC 305. It was the size of two refrigerators, weighed a ton, stored five megabytes of data, and leased for $3,200 per month (roughly $35,000 in today's money). It required its own air conditioning. The machine that made it possible to store and retrieve digital information at scale entered the world the same year you did. In your lifetime, that device shrank from room-sized to invisible — embedded in phones, watches, cameras — and its storage capacity multiplied by a factor that no unit of measurement in 1956 could have expressed.

**Everything happening around your birth traced back to a speech given four months earlier.** In February 1956, Soviet Premier Nikita Khrushchev delivered what became known as the Secret Speech to a closed session of the Communist Party Congress — a four-hour denunciation of Stalin's crimes, his purges, his cult of personality, the terror. It was supposed to be secret. Within months it had leaked, been translated, and was circulating through the communist world. The Poznań uprising and the Hungarian Revolution were both, at least in part, consequences of that speech: if Khrushchev himself said the previous era was criminal, what exactly were people still being asked to obey? You were born into the political earthquake those words set in motion.

---

**The arc of 70 years.**

You were born in a summer of suppressed revolutions and collapsing empires, into a world where storing five megabytes of data required a machine the size of a room. You have lived through the full arc of the digital age — from that first IBM disk drive through the personal computer, the internet, the smartphone, and now the machine that reasons and writes. The hard disk that entered the world the same year you did has been reinvented so many times that its 1956 form is unrecognizable from its current descendants.

The empires that cracked in your birth year — Soviet, British, French — completed their unraveling over the decades of your life. The Cold War ended when you were 33. The Wall fell when you were 33. The Soviet Union dissolved when you were 35.

You were born into the upheaval of 1956, which turned out to be the beginning of a very long process of the old order learning what it could no longer hold. Seventy years later, that process has not finished.
